what_it_does: Multi-task learning (MTL) is a technique where a single neural network is trained to solve several related tasks at once, sharing most of its layers to save parameters and computation. Deploying such a network on a small embedded device (like a microcontroller in a robot or wearable) adds a hard constraint: the network must produce answers fast enough to be useful in real time. Existing automated MTL methods search for good sharing strategies (which layers to share, which to keep separate) without accounting for how long inference will actually take on the target hardware. This paper introduces LA-MTL, which adds an explicit timing cost model — called the Analytical Latency Factor (ALF) — into the search process itself, so the search naturally steers toward designs that are both accurate and fast. The search evaluates latency at a per-layer level during exploration and finds Pareto-optimal solutions (designs where you cannot improve one metric without worsening another) balancing accuracy, model size, and latency. This is based solely on the abstract, so precise numbers should not be assumed accurate.
